title: What to keep from Emerson
hookLine: self-trust, nature, the sacred in the ordinary

cards: A week ends today, and so, almost, does this long walk with Emerson.

This week held Margaret Fuller asking who gets to think, the careful man finally speaking against slavery, a town rebuilding his roof, the old man forgetting names and keeping his gentleness, the masked days holding out their gifts, and yesterday, the fair case against him.
Emerson wouldn't want to be carried around whole. He warned scholars not to let any book, even a great one, do their thinking for them.
So today is a packing question, the kind you ask at the end of a long trip with a small bag: what's worth carrying home?

teach.h: SELF-TRUST: LOOK WITH YOUR OWN EYES.
teach.b: Here are three things some readers keep. First, self-trust. Not selfishness, as this path saw when it read Self-Reliance carefully, but the courage to look with your own eyes.
Emerson's point was that the same light that spoke to the great teachers can speak to you, and that copying someone else's insight is never quite the same as having your own. Second, nature.

In his first book, Nature, he wrote that in the woods a person returns to reason and faith. Some readers still keep that: a walk as a kind of prayer or a kind of clearing, whatever word fits their own path.
Third, the sacred in the ordinary. Some find this one the deepest. In The American Scholar he wrote, "I embrace the common, I explore and sit at the feet of the familiar, the low."
The kitchen, the street, the farm, the walk to work. The holy wasn't hiding far away; it was in plain sight, wearing the mask of an ordinary day, as his poem Days put it.
And the honest fourth: whatever you keep, keep it with yesterday's limits attached. Self-trust beside the neighbors who rebuild. Nature beside the waiting room.
The sacred ordinary beside the people for whom ordinary life is hard.
The point isn't to keep everything.
In his spirit, the advice might be: keep one, and make it yours.

how: Readers who spend time with Emerson often name a few ideas they carry away, such as self-trust, the renewing power of nature, and the holiness of ordinary life.

games.why: he warned scholars not to let a book do their thinking. keeping one idea and making it your own fits that warning.

practice: Lay the three out like objects on a table, self-trust, nature, the sacred in the ordinary, and look at each for a breath or two. Notice which one your hand moves toward, and pick it up without arguing.
Then think of one place in your actual week where it could live: a decision, a walk, a sink full of dishes.
